Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. His apology came in a letter to Nvidia staff, which you can read in full below. Nvidia's board of directors released a statement late on Sunday to address the bombshell report that U.S. intelligence believes Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy . The board says it has no reason to believe sensitive corporate information or U.S. national security was compromised, but the company intends to examine all available information to determine what happened. The BoD claims it is fully confident in Jensen Huang and his leadership team. Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori Huang, for 41 years, says he fully supports the investigation. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," a statement by Nvidia's BoD reads. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. […] Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it." On Friday, the first reporting emerged claiming U.S. intelligence agencies believe Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who was allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) to gather information and help Chinese companies obtain restricted AI GPUs. The company has been on the radar for smuggling restricted hardware to China since at least 2025: Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via its subsidiary Speedmatrix. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. Nvidia has strenuously rejected suggestions of improper dealings, saying that its CEO regularly meets thousands of customers and that these interactions do not involve sensitive corporate information or national security secrets. Chinese officials have also dismissed the espionage allegations as unfounded. The suspected Chinese intelligence operation targeting Jensen has not been independently confirmed as a fact. The relationship is alleged to follow the typical "honeypot" strategy, wherein foreign intelligence agencies use operatives to ensnare targets into romantic relationships to steal information and influence their decision-making. Huang has been an outspoken critic of those opposed to limiting the supply of AI GPUs to China. Huang recently expressed his opinion that the label 'China hawk' is not a badge of honor Americans should wear; it is really 'a badge of shame.' Huang also said it "doesn’t have to be all us or them. It could be us and them," drawing fire from others in the administration and other tech companies, including the CEO of Palantir . My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust." In June 2018, Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich resigned after an internal investigation, assisted by external legal counsel, confirmed that he had engaged in a consensual romantic relationship with an Intel employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. Krzanich, who had led Intel since 2013, also stepped down from the company's board, while then-chief financial officer Robert Swan took over as interim CEO. For now, it remains unclear if Jensen will meet a similar fate and lose control of the company he founded. Jensen's full letter to staff reads as follows: To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. The whole statement from Nvidia's Board of Directors reads as follows: The Nvidia Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. His apology came in a letter to Nvidia staff, which you can read in full below. Nvidia's board of directors released a statement late on Sunday to address the bombshell report that U.S. intelligence believes Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy . The board says it has no reason to believe sensitive corporate information or U.S. national security was compromised, but the company intends to examine all available information to determine what happened.
The BoD claims it is fully confident in Jensen Huang and his leadership team. Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori Huang, for 41 years, says he fully supports the investigation.

"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," a statement by Nvidia's BoD reads. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. […] Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

On Friday, the first reporting emerged claiming U.S. intelligence agencies believe Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who was allegedly recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) to gather information and help Chinese companies obtain restricted AI GPUs. The company has been on the radar for smuggling restricted hardware to China since at least 2025: Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via its subsidiary Speedmatrix.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology.

Nvidia has strenuously rejected suggestions of improper dealings, saying that its CEO regularly meets thousands of customers and that these interactions do not involve sensitive corporate information or national security secrets. Chinese officials have also dismissed the espionage allegations as unfounded.

The suspected Chinese intelligence operation targeting Jensen has not been independently confirmed as a fact. The relationship is alleged to follow the typical "honeypot" strategy, wherein foreign intelligence agencies use operatives to ensnare targets into romantic relationships to steal information and influence their decision-making.

Huang has been an outspoken critic of those opposed to limiting the supply of AI GPUs to China. Huang recently expressed his opinion that the label 'China hawk' is not a badge of honor Americans should wear; it is really 'a badge of shame.' Huang also said it "doesn’t have to be all us or them. It could be us and them," drawing fire from others in the administration and other tech companies, including the CEO of Palantir .

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote . "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust."

In June 2018, Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich resigned after an internal investigation, assisted by external legal counsel, confirmed that he had engaged in a consensual romantic relationship with an Intel employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. Krzanich, who had led Intel since 2013, also stepped down from the company's board, while then-chief financial officer Robert Swan took over as interim CEO. For now, it remains unclear if Jensen will meet a similar fate and lose control of the company he founded.

Jensen's full letter to staff reads as follows: To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

The whole statement from Nvidia's Board of Directors reads as follows: The Nvidia Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.
While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” according to The New York Times .
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.

When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Nvidia’s board “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” Sunday’s company press release read.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”

CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said. There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.”

Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.

“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy.
His apology came in a letter to Nvidia staff, which you can read in full below.

The board says it has no reason to believe sensitive corporate information or U.S. national security was compromised, but the company intends to examine all available information to determine what happened.
"A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation," a statement by Nvidia's BoD reads.
The suspected Chinese intelligence operation targeting Jensen has not been independently confirmed as a fact.

The relationship is alleged to follow the typical "honeypot" strategy, wherein foreign intelligence agencies use operatives to ensnare targets into romantic relationships to steal information and influence their decision-making.
Jensen's full letter to staff reads as follows: To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology.

The company has been on the radar for smuggling restricted hardware to China since at least 2025: Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via its subsidiary Speedmatrix.

In June 2018, Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich resigned after an internal investigation, assisted by external legal counsel, confirmed that he had engaged in a consensual romantic relationship with an Intel employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers.
For now, it remains unclear if Jensen will meet a similar fate and lose control of the company he founded.

Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said.
There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips.
It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday.
“Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.”
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”
The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.

President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.

A statement posted by the board of directors reads: > The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. > The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. > The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips. Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

The statement goes on to impress that the board prioritizes the national and economic security of the United States, and it has no reason to believe “that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” Huang is said to fully support the review.

A New York Times report states that Huang had a relationship with a “tech executive named Alice Huang,” and that “U.S. authorities had concerns about her intelligence connections with China.” The Financial Times then reports that “Alice Huang was in fact a Chinese spy.”

sources.title: Nvidia launches investigation after CEO Jensen Huang admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy - The Independent
passages: Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said.
There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips.
It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday.
“Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.”
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”
The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” according to The New York Times .
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.

When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Nvidia’s board “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” Sunday’s company press release read.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”

CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said. There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.”

Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.

“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

passages: WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that progress had been made toward establishing a postwar security framework for Ukraine and Europe, as US-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine prepare to resume this week in Abu Dhabi with European participation.
“The entirety of the time we’ve been talking about Russia-Ukraine, the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees.

Trump on Thursday predicted a “very big” deal with Moscow involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe,” remarks that raised questions about the potential implications of any settlement for European security.

The security framework has emerged as a central issue in diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, particularly the question of how Ukraine’s security would be protected after any ceasefire or peace agreement and what role European countries and NATO would play.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point.

US envoy Steve Witkoff said Washington would bring Russian and Ukrainian delegations together in the Emirati capital on November 10-11 to discuss ending the war, postwar security arrangements and measures to de-escalate the conflict.

The discussions will test whether Washington can translate the progress reported on security arrangements into a framework acceptable to Kyiv, Moscow and European governments, amid continuing disagreements over the terms of a possible settlement.
Rubio is traveling to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers ahead of the negotiations.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected to represent the United States at the Abu Dhabi talks.

passages: WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that progress had been made toward establishing a postwar security framework for Ukraine and Europe, as US-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine prepare to resume this week in Abu Dhabi with European participation.
“The entirety of the time we’ve been talking about Russia-Ukraine, the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees.

The security framework has emerged as a central issue in diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, particularly the question of how Ukraine’s security would be protected after any ceasefire or peace agreement and what role European countries and NATO would play.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point.

The discussions will test whether Washington can translate the progress reported on security arrangements into a framework acceptable to Kyiv, Moscow and European governments, amid continuing disagreements over the terms of a possible settlement.
Rubio is traveling to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers ahead of the negotiations.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected to represent the United States at the Abu Dhabi talks.

Rubio's comments, ahead of his travel to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, come as Russia-Ukraine negotiations under US mediation have been set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi.
US President Donald Trump on Thursday predicted a "very big" deal with Moscow involving not only Ukraine but "all of Europe," in remarks likely to fuel fresh fears of a pivot towards the Kremlin.
Zelensky says ready for talks on 'ceasefire formats'

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by the New York Times.

extraction.body: US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company. Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders. Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years. He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American." A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." US President Donald Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he now wished he had "acted on the intelligence" at the time, Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting the Nvidia chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation" . Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and he took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did. His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions. This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta. The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever. US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by the New York Times. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship. Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said. Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state". China Media Group, which acknowledged Mbappé's apology, has not said how long the blackout will last. US intelligence officials believe a Chinese businesswoman was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, The New York Times reports. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife,” according to The New York Times .
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Late last month, the Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.

Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.

When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Nvidia’s board “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” Sunday’s company press release read.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information.”

CEO Huang supports the investigation and has agreed to cooperate, the board said. There was no word of Huang’s position being in jeopardy, with the board saying it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.”

Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.

“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

extraction.body: US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company. Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders. Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years. He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American." A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." US President Donald Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he now wished he had "acted on the intelligence" at the time, Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting the Nvidia chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation" . Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and he took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did. His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions. This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta. The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever. US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by the New York Times. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship. Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said. Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state". China Media Group, which acknowledged Mbappé's apology, has not said how long the blackout will last. Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

The U.S. Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees. In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang. They stated, "Recent reports raise serious national security concerns regarding the possibility of China accessing sensitive U.S. technologies and information," adding, "The issues of Chinese infiltration and access to advanced U.S. technology are core investigative matters for the three committees during this session." They emphasized, "It is crucial for Congress to understand the extent to which U.S. national security has been exposed to risk." This request indicates growing congressional pressure surrounding the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is suspected of Chinese espionage. Alice Huang is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-headquartered data center company. She was photographed drinking alongside Jensen Huang and other artificial intelligence (AI) company executives at a bar in Taiwan in June 2024, and was spotted with him again in May of last year. Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds. Previously, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Alice Huang is suspected of maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang and leaking information to China. The NYT also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the matter by intelligence agencies but took no action. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that authorities in at least three countries are concerned that Alice Huang may have leaked sensitive information regarding Nvidia chips to the Chinese government. However, Nvidia has denied the allegations, stating that Jensen Huang's contact with Alice Huang was merely routine business interaction and that no national security-related information was leaked. Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons. The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added. The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips. Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added. The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him. The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity. Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern. The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed. Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter. The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. extraction.body: The chief executive of one of the world's largest public corporations is facing an inquiry following reports he conducted an 'affair' with an alleged Chinese spy. Jensen Huang serves as chief executive officer of Nvidia, presently ranked second only to Apple amongst the globe's largest publicly traded firms, and is reported to have acknowledged the affair. The $4.5 trillion American technology giant initiated the independent inquiry after reports emerged that its founder and CEO had become the subject of a 'foreign intelligence effort', the Nvidia Board of Directors confirmed in a statement. The New York Times referenced US intelligence officials who identified businesswoman Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese operative. Jensen Huang has now acknowledged he was "unfaithful" to his wife and expressed remorse for the pain he has inflicted upon her and their children, according to subsequent reports. Meanwhile, Nvidia's Board stated it possessed no grounds to suspect that company secrets or US national security had been jeopardised - and indicated Mr Huang remained committed to continuing his leadership of the business. Nvidia ranks amongst the world's most valuable corporations and is regarded as pivotal to manufacturing the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with Mr Huang having led it for over three decades. The announcement followed Mr Huang's admission to the board that he had been intimate with a Chinese business executive, whom US intelligence identified as collecting information for Beijing, The New York Times reported. Mr Huang issued an apology in a message to the firm, the Times reported. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Nvidia's board stated it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but confirmed its investigation would scrutinise all available evidence. Mr Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to co-operating with it," the board said. Mr Huang, 63, will continue as chief executive throughout the probe. The Times disclosed last month that US intelligence services had uncovered that Mr Huang had formed a close association with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and chip purchaser, and concluded that she was passing intelligence straight to Beijing. The pair are not related, the Times confirmed. Alice Huang previously worked as a television journalist in China before rising to senior executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, which has emerged as one of Nvidia's largest clients in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed purchased more than 4.8 billion US dollars (£3.6 billion) worth of Nvidia chips during the past two years, the Times reported. In a statement issued in recent hours, the Nvidia Board announced: "The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. "The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

Jensen Huang serves as chief executive officer of Nvidia, presently ranked second only to Apple amongst the globe's largest publicly traded firms, and is reported to have acknowledged the affair. The $4.5 trillion American technology giant initiated the independent inquiry after reports emerged that its founder and CEO had become the subject of a 'foreign intelligence effort', the Nvidia Board of Directors confirmed in a statement. The New York Times referenced US intelligence officials who identified businesswoman Alice Huang as a suspected Chinese operative. Jensen Huang has now acknowledged he was "unfaithful" to his wife and expressed remorse for the pain he has inflicted upon her and their children, according to subsequent reports. Meanwhile, Nvidia's Board stated it possessed no grounds to suspect that company secrets or US national security had been jeopardised - and indicated Mr Huang remained committed to continuing his leadership of the business. Nvidia ranks amongst the world's most valuable corporations and is regarded as pivotal to manufacturing the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with Mr Huang having led it for over three decades. The announcement followed Mr Huang's admission to the board that he had been intimate with a Chinese business executive, whom US intelligence identified as collecting information for Beijing, The New York Times reported. Mr Huang issued an apology in a message to the firm, the Times reported. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Nvidia's board stated it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but confirmed its investigation would scrutinise all available evidence. Mr Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to co-operating with it," the board said. Mr Huang, 63, will continue as chief executive throughout the probe. The Times disclosed last month that US intelligence services had uncovered that Mr Huang had formed a close association with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and chip purchaser, and concluded that she was passing intelligence straight to Beijing. The pair are not related, the Times confirmed. Alice Huang previously worked as a television journalist in China before rising to senior executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, which has emerged as one of Nvidia's largest clients in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed purchased more than 4.8 billion US dollars (£3.6 billion) worth of Nvidia chips during the past two years, the Times reported. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. "Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. "The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

Blades Brown has made PGA Tour history after becoming the youngest winner on the circuit since 1931, defeating Ben James in a dramatic playoff at the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship. The 19-year-old American produced a sensational final-round comeback at Tiger Woods' El Cardonal at Diamante in Los Cabos, Mexico, to claim his maiden PGA Tour title and a huge $1.08 million first prize. Brown, who secured his PGA Tour card through the Korn Ferry Tour last month, began Sunday's final round seven shots off the pace, with James holding a four-shot advantage over the chasing pack. However, Brown fired a stunning 9-under 63 featuring 10 birdies to storm up the leaderboard and force his way into contention. James looked to have thrown the tournament away before producing a remarkable eagle on the par-5 18th, holing a 20-foot putt to force a playoff with both players finishing at 23-under-par . After matching birdies on the first extra hole, the pair returned to the 18th. James missed his birdie attempt from seven feet, allowing Brown to convert from three feet and seal a remarkable victory. At 19 years, five months and 18 days old, Brown becomes the youngest PGA Tour winner since Charles Kocsis triumphed at the 1931 Michigan Open. He also moves ahead of Jordan Spieth, who was 19 years, 11 months and 17 days old when he won the 2013 John Deere Classic. Brown is now the fourth-youngest winner in PGA Tour history. The American spoke exclusively to GolfMagic back in August. "It's crazy," Brown said after his historic triumph. "I just think back to all the people in my life, my parents, my sister, my coach, there's so many people that believe in me, and to finally get the first one under my belt is pretty special." Brown added: "I'm just obsessed with this game. It tests you in so many different ways, I think it's a good metaphor for life. "I love golf, I love all the stuff that goes into it, and I can't wait for what's next." The victory earns Brown a two-year PGA Tour exemption, a place in the 2028 Championship Series and invitations to the 2027 Players Championship and PGA Championship. James, meanwhile, takes home $534,000 after another impressive top-10 finish, although the 23-year-old will be disappointed to have missed out on his maiden Tour title. With just two events remaining in the FedExCup Fall Series, players will continue battling for PGA Tour cards and 2027 eligibility status. James looked to have thrown the tournament away before producing a remarkable eagle on the par-5 18th, holing a 20-foot putt to force a playoff with both players finishing at 23-under-par .
After matching birdies on the first extra hole, the pair returned to the 18th.
James missed his birdie attempt from seven feet, allowing Brown to convert from three feet and seal a remarkable victory.
At 19 years, five months and 18 days old, Brown becomes the youngest PGA Tour winner since Charles Kocsis triumphed at the 1931 Michigan Open.

The American spoke exclusively to GolfMagic back in August.

"I love golf, I love all the stuff that goes into it, and I can't wait for what's next."
The victory earns Brown a two-year PGA Tour exemption, a place in the 2028 Championship Series and invitations to the 2027 Players Championship and PGA Championship.
James, meanwhile, takes home $534,000 after another impressive top-10 finish, although the 23-year-old will be disappointed to have missed out on his maiden Tour title.
With just two events remaining in the FedExCup Fall Series, players will continue battling for PGA Tour cards and 2027 eligibility status.
For Brown, however, his breakthrough victory in Mexico marks the beginning of what promises to be an exciting PGA Tour career.

The 19-year-old from Tennessee -- who skipped college to turn professional straight out of high school -- had begun the final day a giant seven strokes back, tied for ninth, but recorded the day's lowest round with 10 birdies in Cabo San Lucas. Brown held his nerve to sink a six-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole for the solo clubhouse lead at 23-under par, with overnight leader Ben James still on the course and two strokes back. After a string of pars, James needed an eagle on the par-five 18th. He fired a superb approach iron to within 20 feet and sank the putt to force a sudden-death playoff on the same hole. Both men found the middle of the green in two. James, going first from 27 feet, missed by inches, but Brown left his slightly easier putt just short. Repeating the hole, both left their approaches short and right. But after a fine chip, James pushed his six-foot putt wide right, and Brown sank his for victory. "Playoff holes are just... they're incredible. It tests you in so many different ways," said Brown, who had a lengthy wait between the end of his round and the playoff. "I was hitting balls and saw he made it, and I was like, 'All right, playoff, let's go.' "I've known Ben since we were amateur golfers, and he's just such an unbelievable player. He's lights-out with the putter. "I got him this time, but I'm sure we're going to be battling out years to come." At 19 years and five months, Brown is the fourth-youngest PGA Tour winner in history, surpassing Jordan Spieth's victory at the 2013 John Deere Classic at 19 years and 11 months as the youngest in modern times. Michael Kim finished third, one stroke back at 22-under-par, having birdied the final hole moments before his Sunday playing partner Brown followed suit to retake the lead. Japan's Kensei Hirata was fourth at 21-under, with David Ford fifth a further stroke back. After his unusual decision to skip college, Brown missed the cut on his pro debut aged 17 at last year's PGA Tour American Express in La Quinta. He was ranked 485th in the world at the start of this year, but has had a stellar campaign. Brown made headlines with his 12-under par 60 at La Quinta this January, which saw him share the halfway lead with world number one and eventual champion Scottie Scheffler. He also finished third at this year's Puerto Rico Open. Brown recorded two runner-up finishes on the Korn Ferry Tour, last month becoming the youngest player ever to earn a PGA Tour card through the developmental series. "It's crazy... to finally get my first one under my ball is pretty special," said Brown.

extraction.body: LOS CABOS, Mexico — Blades Brown is like several young players who can remember Tiger Woods making big putts and winning big tournaments and inspiring them to play. Only for Brown, it wasn't all that long ago. Two years after his surprising decision to turn pro while a junior in high school, the 19-year-old Brown became the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years when he closed with a 9-under 63 and beat Ben James on the second playoff hole in the World Wide Technology Championship. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “I just go back to 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind-blowing.” Brown is the youngest winner since Charles Kocsis won the Michigan Open in 1931 when he was 18, a tournament that was considered a regional event in the early years of the PGA. James lost a four-shot lead going into the final round at El Cardonal at Diamante and then showed his moxie by smoking a 285-yard shot into 20 feet on the par-5 18th and making eagle to salvage a 70 and force the playoff. But he missed an 8-foot putt on the second playoff hole, and Brown made his 3-footer. “Had a feeling that it was going to go in,” James said of his clutch eagle, the only putt he made all day longer than 15 feet. “Hadn’t really made anything all day. Just had a really good line on it and it was a good putt. Played the best I could.” For a sleepy FedEx Cup Fall event on the southern tip of Baja California, this was pure theater between two players from the next generation. James was the No. 1 player in the PGA Tour University ranking last season. Brown turned pro at 17 and earned his PGA Tour card this year by being among the top 20 in Korn Ferry Tour points. He made up a seven-shot deficit in the final round and then was tested even more by going through two bags of golf balls on the range, waiting to see if the two-shot lead he had over James would hold. Then it was back to the par-5 18th for the playoff. On the first extra hole, their approach shots were side-by-side, separated by about 3 feet, and both narrowly missed eagle chances. They returned to the 18th tee and their drives were next to each other. Both came up just short of the green. James nearly holed his pitch and saw it run out 8 feet. Brown, who had a similar pitch in regulation that he hit to 6 feet for a closing birdie, this time came up 3 feet short. James' birdie putt grazed the right edge, and Brown poured in the winner. “I’m so obsessed with this game. It tests you in so many ways,” Brown said. “I love golf, all the stuff that goes into it and I can’t wait for what’s next.” With eight players separated by two shots on the back nine, Brown ran off three straight birdies to share the lead and then left the mistakes to everyone else. He hit a superb pitch for birdie on the final hole to post at 23-under 265. That put him one shot ahead of Michael Kim, who played with the Tennessee teen and made birdie from 12 feet for 64 right before Brown made his putt. Brown now has a two-year exemption, which puts him in the elite Championship Series when the PGA Tour's new model begins in 2028. The victory also assures Brown of his first major next year at the PGA Championship. It was another setback for James, who in 13 starts since turning pro has five finishes in the top five, and two runner-up finishes. Denny McCarthy, winless in nine years in 240 starts on the PGA Tour, made a 30-foot birdie putt on the 13th hole to take the lead. But he hit a pedestrian pitch to the par-5 14th and had to settle for par. With a wedge in hand from the 15th fairway, he came up some 40 feet short and three-putted for a bogey. McCarthy's tee shot on the 17th was right of the 18th tee box; he put his next shot off a dirt path into a hazard and made double bogey. He shot 69.

extraction.body: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo. In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times. In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour. James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours. While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh. Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.” Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories. Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years. Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.” It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race. Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler. When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler. Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too. James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes. “Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.” Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under. passages: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo.

In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times.
In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour.

James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours.

While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh.

Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old.

“It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.”

Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories.

Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years.
Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.”

It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race.

Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler.

When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler.
Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too.

James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes.

“Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.”

Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under.

James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole.

“If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’”
