coreStoryFacts.text: Blades Brown has made PGA Tour history after becoming the youngest winner on the circuit since 1931, defeating Ben James in a dramatic playoff at the 2026 World Wide Technology Championship.
The victory earns Brown a two-year PGA Tour exemption, a place in the 2028 Championship Series and invitations to the 2027 Players Championship and PGA Championship.

The 19-year-old American produced a sensational final-round comeback at Tiger Woods' El Cardonal at Diamante in Los Cabos, Mexico, to claim his maiden PGA Tour title and a huge $1.08 million first prize.
For Brown, however, his breakthrough victory in Mexico marks the beginning of what promises to be an exciting PGA Tour career.
Andy Roberts first joined GolfMagic on a month's work experience back in April 2011.
The American spoke exclusively to GolfMagic back in August.

Teenage sensation Blades Brown became the PGA Tour's youngest winner since 1931 as he stormed to a playoff victory at the World Wide Technology Championship in Mexico after a stunning nine-under par 63 on Sunday.
Brown recorded two runner-up finishes on the Korn Ferry Tour, last month becoming the youngest player ever to earn a PGA Tour card through the developmental series.
After his unusual decision to skip college, Brown missed the cut on his pro debut aged 17 at last year's PGA Tour American Express in La Quinta.
James, going first from 27 feet, missed by inches, but Brown left his slightly easier putt just short.
Brown held his nerve to sink a six-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole for the solo clubhouse lead at 23-under par, with overnight leader Ben James still on the course and two strokes back.

Two years after his surprising decision to turn pro while a junior in high school, the 19-year-old Brown became the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years when he closed with a 9-under 63 and beat Ben James on the second playoff hole in the World Wide Technology Championship.
For a sleepy FedEx Cup Fall event on the southern tip of Baja California, this was pure theater between two players from the next generation.
Brown turned pro at 17 and earned his PGA Tour card this year by being among the top 20 in Korn Ferry Tour points.
The victory also assures Brown of his first major next year at the PGA Championship.
But he hit a pedestrian pitch to the par-5 14th and had to settle for par.
LOS CABOS, Mexico — Blades Brown is like several young players who can remember Tiger Woods making big putts and winning big tournaments and inspiring them to play.
James' birdie putt grazed the right edge, and Brown poured in the winner.
It was another setback for James, who in 13 starts since turning pro has five finishes in the top five, and two runner-up finishes.

The 19-year-old from Tennessee -- who skipped college to turn professional straight out of high school -- had begun the final day a giant seven strokes back, tied for ninth, but recorded the day's lowest round with 10 birdies in Cabo San Lucas. Brown held his nerve to sink a six-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole for the solo clubhouse lead at 23-under par, with overnight leader Ben James still on the course and two strokes back. After a string of pars, James needed an eagle on the par-five 18th. He fired a superb approach iron to within 20 feet and sank the putt to force a sudden-death playoff on the same hole. Both men found the middle of the green in two. James, going first from 27 feet, missed by inches, but Brown left his slightly easier putt just short. Repeating the hole, both left their approaches short and right. But after a fine chip, James pushed his six-foot putt wide right, and Brown sank his for victory. "Playoff holes are just... they're incredible. It tests you in so many different ways," said Brown, who had a lengthy wait between the end of his round and the playoff. "I was hitting balls and saw he made it, and I was like, 'All right, playoff, let's go.' "I've known Ben since we were amateur golfers, and he's just such an unbelievable player. He's lights-out with the putter. "I got him this time, but I'm sure we're going to be battling out years to come." At 19 years and five months, Brown is the fourth-youngest PGA Tour winner in history, surpassing Jordan Spieth's victory at the 2013 John Deere Classic at 19 years and 11 months as the youngest in modern times. Michael Kim finished third, one stroke back at 22-under-par, having birdied the final hole moments before his Sunday playing partner Brown followed suit to retake the lead. Japan's Kensei Hirata was fourth at 21-under, with David Ford fifth a further stroke back. After his unusual decision to skip college, Brown missed the cut on his pro debut aged 17 at last year's PGA Tour American Express in La Quinta. He was ranked 485th in the world at the start of this year, but has had a stellar campaign. Brown made headlines with his 12-under par 60 at La Quinta this January, which saw him share the halfway lead with world number one and eventual champion Scottie Scheffler. He also finished third at this year's Puerto Rico Open. Brown recorded two runner-up finishes on the Korn Ferry Tour, last month becoming the youngest player ever to earn a PGA Tour card through the developmental series. "It's crazy... to finally get my first one under my ball is pretty special," said Brown.

(Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images)
It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old.
He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race.
Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour.

Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old.
“It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said.
James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer.

He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make.
James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No.
13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes.

Brown was almost in the exact spot that James was in regulation, at about 20 feet from the cup.
James’ eagle bid tried to curl back right into the hole but failed, Brown’s try came up a few revolutions short, and the two headed back to the 18th tee.
“I’ve known Ben since we were amateur golfers and he’s just such a great player,” Brown said.
Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.”
In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No.
Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too.
James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own.

extraction.body: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo. In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times. In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour. James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours. While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh. Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.” Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories. Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years. Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.” It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race. Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler. When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler. Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too. James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes. “Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.” Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under. Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt. “I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.” James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole. “If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’” CABO SAN LUCAS, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 08: Blades Brown of the United States celebrates with his dad, Parke Brown, after winning the final round of the World Wide Technology Championship 2026 at El Cardonal at Diamante on November 08, 2026 in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) On the first playoff hole, No. 18, James hit his second shot nearly to the same spot, just a few feet farther away. Brown was almost in the exact spot that James was in regulation, at about 20 feet from the cup. James’ eagle bid tried to curl back right into the hole but failed, Brown’s try came up a few revolutions short, and the two headed back to the 18th tee. Both players nearly hit their next tee shots into their own divots, though neither found the green in two this time, both missing short and right. James nearly chipped in, but he ran it too far past for his balky putter and whiffed on the 6-footer. Brown cozied one close and didn’t miss his opportunity to break through. “I’ve known Ben since we were amateur golfers and he’s just such a great player,” Brown said. “I’m sure we’re going to be battling it out for years to come.” Not long after he shook James’ hand on the final green, Brown was getting bear-hugged by his dad, Parke, who rarely skips a tournament. Parke actually missed two while undergoing chemotherapy a few years ago for hairy cell leukemia. Parke was initially misdiagnosed and given months to live, but he now manages the treatable disease while traveling the world with his only son, who is now a PGA Tour champion with the golf world seemingly at his fingertips. Blades, who inherited his dad’s infectious energy and charisma, balks somewhat at the projections, which are even loftier now. “I’ve got a long way to go,” Brown said. “There’s so many shots that I want to learn. Golf, I don’t think you ever can master, but I’m going to do my best to see how close we can get.” © Copyright 2026 Golf Channel. All rights reserved.

passages: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo.

In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times.
In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour.

James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours.

While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh.

Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old.

“It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.”

Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories.

Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years.
Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.”

It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race.

Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler.

When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler.
Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too.

James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes.

“Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.”

Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under.

Brown had birdied nine of his first 15 holes, three coming from about 12 feet and two more from around 25 feet – not surprising considering Brown is used to converting from deep; his mother, Rhonda, made the first 3-pointer in WNBA history while her son was a standout guard in high school. Blades claims he once almost made 50 consecutive 3’s during a shootaround.

Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt.

“I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.”

James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole.

extraction.body: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo. In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times. In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour. James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours. While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh. Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.” Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories. Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years. Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.” It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race. Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler. When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler. Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too. James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes. “Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.” Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under. Brown had birdied nine of his first 15 holes, three coming from about 12 feet and two more from around 25 feet – not surprising considering Brown is used to converting from deep; his mother, Rhonda, made the first 3-pointer in WNBA history while her son was a standout guard in high school. Blades claims he once almost made 50 consecutive 3’s during a shootaround. Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt. “I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.” James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole. “If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’” CABO SAN LUCAS, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 08: Blades Brown of the United States celebrates with his dad, Parke Brown, after winning the final round of the World Wide Technology Championship 2026 at El Cardonal at Diamante on November 08, 2026 in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) On the first playoff hole, No. 18, James hit his second shot nearly to the same spot, just a few feet farther away. Brown was almost in the exact spot that James was in regulation, at about 20 feet from the cup. James’ eagle bid tried to curl back right into the hole but failed, Brown’s try came up a few revolutions short, and the two headed back to the 18th tee. Both players nearly hit their next tee shots into their own divots, though neither found the green in two this time, both missing short and right. James nearly chipped in, but he ran it too far past for his balky putter and whiffed on the 6-footer. passages: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo.

In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times.
In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour.

James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours.

While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh.

Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old.

“It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.”

Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories.

Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years.
Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.”

It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race.

Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler.

When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler.
Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too.

James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes.

“Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.”

Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under.

Brown had birdied nine of his first 15 holes, three coming from about 12 feet and two more from around 25 feet – not surprising considering Brown is used to converting from deep; his mother, Rhonda, made the first 3-pointer in WNBA history while her son was a standout guard in high school. Blades claims he once almost made 50 consecutive 3’s during a shootaround.

Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt.

“I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.”

James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole.

“If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’”

Bitcoin has demonstrated remarkable growth, gaining 10,587% over the past decade, as reported by Bilello, averaging about 59% per year. Reaching $2 million by 2035 would require slower growth than this historical performance, while a 2030 goal would require a significantly higher growth rate.

Currently, Bitcoin is on track for its fifth consecutive weekly loss, dropping from a close of $86,507 in the week of October 4 to about $75,662. It traded as low as $74,722 this week. According to Hedgeye, the cryptocurrency reached an eight-week low below $76,000 on November 5.

Bitcoin is trading below both its 20-day average of $79,362 and its 50-day average of $81,889, suggesting short-term sellers are in control. The next support level, where buyers typically appear, is the 200-day average at $73,194, which is roughly 3% below the current price.

Even optimistic analysts have raised concerns about this situation. Jordi Visser said on September 19 that "If bitcoin is below 80,000 by the end of October, there's a problem," and Bitcoin finished October close to $77,474.

To gauge the potential depth of the next major drop, consider the last major decline, when Bitcoin fell to a close of $58,566 on June 30, marking its lowest closing price over the previous year. A similar drop could breach the 200-day average and push Bitcoin back toward that June low.

The likelihood of Bitcoin reaching $2 million by 2030 appears very slim, and the chance is still low for 2035. Beth Kindig, a tech analyst at the I/O Fund, expects Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) to drop again before rallying, but she also projects it could reach $2 million. “We believe that one more large drop is coming over the next several months,” she shared on X on November 6, 2026.
She also noted, “Our long-term thesis for Bitcoin reaching $2 million remains intact, but the path is unlikely to be a straight line.”

Bitcoin is trading at approximately $75,662 on November 8, which is down 8% over the last 30 days and 13.3% in 2026. This decline follows a peak of $84,082 on October 21. According to Charlie Bilello, Bitcoin and gold have been the two worst-performing major assets this year.

Kindig associates her caution with fluctuations in currency markets. In a post on November 5, she explained that the dollar is trending higher and bond yields are rising. She remarked, “Two months later, $BTC peaked, and it has since fallen 54%.” Bitcoin is about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080, reached on October 6, 2025, so her 54% likely measures the fall to the June 30 closing low of $58,566.
So, can Bitcoin truly reach $2 million, representing a 26-fold increase from its current $75,000 price? And what timeline would this require?

If Bitcoin reaches $2 million per coin, its market value would soar to around $40 trillion, up from approximately $1.52 trillion now. The market cap is calculated by multiplying the price by the number of coins in circulation. Currently, 20,109,575 of the total 21 million Bitcoins are already circulating. Since most of the supply has already been released, any significant price increase would require substantial new investments in a relatively fixed supply.

This projected valuation would far exceed gold holdings, as major financial institutions have noted. For example, JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) estimates private-sector gold holdings at about $8 trillion, while its volatility-adjusted model places Bitcoin’s fair value at about $5.3 trillion, or about $266,000 per coin.

While Kindig believes in Bitcoin’s potential, she hasn’t specified a timeline for reaching $2 million. The timeline is crucial in determining how steep the rise needs to be. To hit the $2 million target by 2030, Bitcoin would need to grow by approximately 127% each year. If the timeline extends to 2035, the annual growth requirement decreases to around 44%.

Bitcoin has demonstrated remarkable growth, gaining 10,587% over the past decade, as reported by Bilello, averaging about 59% per year. Reaching $2 million by 2035 would require slower growth than this historical performance, while a 2030 goal would require a significantly higher growth rate.

Currently, Bitcoin is on track for its fifth consecutive weekly loss, dropping from a close of $86,507 in the week of October 4 to about $75,662. It traded as low as $74,722 this week. According to Hedgeye, the cryptocurrency reached an eight-week low below $76,000 on November 5.

Even optimistic analysts have raised concerns about this situation. Jordi Visser said on September 19 that “If bitcoin is below 80,000 by the end of October, there’s a problem,” and Bitcoin finished October close to $77,474.

To gauge the potential depth of the next major drop, consider the last major decline, when Bitcoin fell to a close of $58,566 on June 30, marking its lowest closing price over the previous year. A similar drop could breach the 200-day average and push Bitcoin back toward that June low.

In her November 6 post, Kindig emphasized that global liquidity is a key driver for Bitcoin’s price. The M2 money supply, which includes cash, checking, savings, and money market funds, rose to $23.41 trillion in September, up 0.5% from August and from $22.25 trillion in November 2025.

However, despite the rise in the U.S. money supply, Bitcoin’s value fell 25.8% over the year, suggesting a stronger dollar and rising yields may be outpacing any positive effects of increased liquidity.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs let stock market investors buy Bitcoin through brokerage accounts, driving significant capital inflows. They received inflows of $526.6 million on October 19 and $528.4 million on October 21, coinciding with Bitcoin’s 30-day high close of $84,082.

The likelihood of Bitcoin reaching $2 million by 2030 appears very slim, and the chance is still low for 2035. Reaching $2 million by 2030 would require an annual growth rate of about 127%, more than twice the 59% average Bitcoin has seen over the past decade. First, Bitcoin must stabilize at its 200-day average of $73,194 before it can advance.

extraction.body: Apple’s new CEO is pressing software chief Craig Federighi to take a more ambitious approach to AI as the company looks to transform Siri into an autonomous agent that can get things done for users. Bloomberg reported the plan on November 8. The report suggests Apple wants Siri to move beyond answering questions and basic commands. Instead, Siri could become an agent that can complete tasks across apps, devices, and services. That could mean asking Siri to plan a trip, manage a shopping list, book a table, or handle a work task without opening multiple apps. The idea fits a broader industry shift toward AI agents that can act on a user’s behalf. For Apple, the challenge is to make Siri genuinely useful while protecting privacy. Apple has traditionally emphasized on-device processing, so users may expect strong controls over what Siri can access and remember. The report also comes as Apple faces pressure to prove that its AI strategy can drive future growth. The company has been adding AI features across iPhones, iPads, and Macs, including new Siri capabilities and stronger on-device AI processing. For users, the potential benefit is convenience. A more capable Siri could make everyday tasks easier, especially if it can understand context and complete multi-step actions. For developers, the shift could create new opportunities to build apps that work with Apple’s AI systems. But they will need clear rules about data access, permissions, and user control. The report suggests that Apple may be preparing a bigger AI push, even if the company has been slower than some rivals to launch advanced AI features. extraction.body: Breaking News Apple CEO John Ternus has reportedly told software chief Craig Federighi that improving Siri is no longer enough, pressing him to accelerate Apple’s broader artificial intelligence strategy amid concerns the company is falling behind its rivals. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Federighi in recent weeks to push for a more ambitious AI roadmap. The reported discussion reflects frustration over what Ternus sees as a lack of urgency compared with other technology companies. Apple has not publicly confirmed the meeting or the account of what was said. The intervention is notable because Ternus only recently became Apple’s chief executive, succeeding Tim Cook in September. extraction.body: Apple’s new CEO is pressing software chief Craig Federighi to take a more ambitious approach to AI as the company looks to transform Siri into an autonomous agent that can get things done for users. Bloomberg reported the plan on November 8. The report suggests Apple wants Siri to move beyond answering questions and basic commands. Instead, Siri could become an agent that can complete tasks across apps, devices, and services. That could mean asking Siri to plan a trip, manage a shopping list, book a table, or handle a work task without opening multiple apps. The idea fits a broader industry shift toward AI agents that can act on a user’s behalf. For Apple, the challenge is to make Siri genuinely useful while protecting privacy. Apple has traditionally emphasized on-device processing, so users may expect strong controls over what Siri can access and remember. The report also comes as Apple faces pressure to prove that its AI strategy can drive future growth. The company has been adding AI features across iPhones, iPads, and Macs, including new Siri capabilities and stronger on-device AI processing. For users, the potential benefit is convenience. A more capable Siri could make everyday tasks easier, especially if it can understand context and complete multi-step actions. For developers, the shift could create new opportunities to build apps that work with Apple’s AI systems. But they will need clear rules about data access, permissions, and user control. The report suggests that Apple may be preparing a bigger AI push, even if the company has been slower than some rivals to launch advanced AI features. passages: Breaking News Apple CEO John Ternus has reportedly told software chief Craig Federighi that improving Siri is no longer enough, pressing him to accelerate Apple’s broader artificial intelligence strategy amid concerns the company is falling behind its rivals.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Federighi in recent weeks to push for a more ambitious AI roadmap. The reported discussion reflects frustration over what Ternus sees as a lack of urgency compared with other technology companies. Apple has not publicly confirmed the meeting or the account of what was said.

The intervention is notable because Ternus only recently became Apple’s chief executive, succeeding Tim Cook in September. It suggests the company’s new leader wants AI to become a bigger priority across Apple’s software rather than remain primarily a project to modernize Siri.

Federighi oversees software engineering and took charge of Apple’s AI efforts after a leadership shake-up last year. The rebuilt Siri AI has since reached customers, with features including personal context, understanding of information on screen and more sophisticated actions in apps. However, those improvements largely remain focused on responding to commands initiated by users.

Apple is now reportedly exploring how Siri could become a more autonomous AI agent capable of following a goal and making progress on tasks without needing a separate instruction at every step. That would put it closer to emerging agent-based services from rival companies. The Apple Post’s guide to Siri AI in iOS 27 details the capabilities available today, which are distinct from the more ambitious direction now under consideration.

Gurman’s reporting indicates that Ternus wants Apple to look further ahead than incremental Siri updates. The company has not announced an autonomous version of Siri, and there is no confirmed release date or final list of features. Any future system would also face challenges around privacy, permissions and how much authority it should have to act on behalf of an iPhone owner.

Bloomberg also describes friction surrounding Federighi’s management approach. He reportedly takes a close interest in technical decisions and debates proposals in detail, a style that some employees believe leaves limited room for other voices to influence the direction of Apple’s products. That account is based on the report’s sources, not a public assessment by Apple.

Planning horizons are another point of tension. Federighi’s organization is said to work largely within a 12- to 18-month window, while Apple’s hardware teams plan products several years into the future. A shorter software roadmap could make it harder to develop ambitious AI experiences that need sustained coordination across devices, operating systems and services.

The pressure arrives as Apple is also experimenting with how it builds its next operating systems. Bloomberg reports that the first iOS 28 development milestone gives engineers more time for coding and exploration before integrating features into the wider release. The adjustment is a separate part of Apple’s software strategy, and it does not establish which new AI features will ship.

Further changes could involve personnel as well as software. Bloomberg reports that Mike Rockwell, Apple’s vice president of Siri engineering and a key figure behind Vision Pro, continues to consider stepping down from his position or leaving the company next year. No departure has been announced, and there is no indication in the reporting that Federighi is preparing to leave.

For Apple customers, the clearest near-term test will be whether the Siri features already introduced and those still in development become reliable, useful parts of everyday work. A more capable autonomous assistant would mark a much larger shift, but Ternus’s reported push is an internal strategic direction rather than a product announcement.

The stakes are growing as rival AI services move from answering questions toward carrying out complex tasks. Under Ternus, Apple now appears to be confronting a larger decision: how quickly it can turn its privacy-focused software and device ecosystem into a platform for the next generation of AI. Whether that urgency translates into new products and features remains to be seen.

extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.

So can a cap this small move either coin’s price?
While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain.

Under a new Bank of Russia regulation, investors who aren’t classified as professional buyers can start buying Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), and the Tether ( CRYPTO:USDT ) stablecoin from November 17. Bitcoin trades at $75,662 and Ethereum at $2,226 today. So can a cap this small move either coin’s price? The regulation has been officially released, naming the three cryptocurrencies eligible for purchase, the start date, and the cap for each intermediary. All buyers will also need to pass a knowledge test before investing. Qualified investors, on the other hand, face no purchase limits. While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain. In October, the Bank of Russia authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to provide crypto exchange services. On November 2, Moscow Exchange announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades. However, Russia hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast. Since the 300,000-ruble cap applies to each intermediary, a buyer with accounts at several brokers could buy more than the cap in a year. That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper. Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand. Because of OFAC sanctions, Coinbase can’t serve Russian customers, so it won’t earn any direct revenue from the new regulation. Russian buying could only help Coinbase through higher crypto prices, which could in turn lift its trading and subscription income. Against Coinbase’s third-quarter revenue of $1.22 billion, any such increase would be minimal. Our Coinbase stock outlook looks at what moves the shares. Strategy holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers. Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access. Russia’s new rules support that view, but Strategy’s stock closely follows Bitcoin’s price. Given that the cap applies inside a sanctioned country, the rule is unlikely to meaningfully move Bitcoin’s market value. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows in the week to November 6. To offset that one week of outflows, about 350,000 Russian buyers would each need to buy the full annual cap. History points the same way. When El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply. Similarly, the launch of Hong Kong’s spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs in April 2024 didn’t lead to sustained price gains. Russia also plans to ban peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. So some of the new regulated buying could come from existing Russian traders moving off informal channels ahead of that ban, rather than from new investors. On the current evidence, the 300,000-ruble cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit. Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential Russian buying. Ethereum also trades below its 30-day low close of $2,236, and capped Russian buyers might prefer Bitcoin, the better-known coin. If Bitcoin fails to reclaim its $79,362 20-day average before Moscow Exchange’s December 1 launch, that would suggest the new rules had little effect on its price. For Ethereum, the key level is its $2,156 200-day average, about 3% below its price. Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers. Russia’s central bank opened the crypto market to retail investors. Under a new Bank of Russia regulation, investors who aren’t classified as professional buyers can start buying Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), and the Tether ( CRYPTO:USDT ) stablecoin from November 17. However, purchases through any one intermediary are capped at 300,000 rubles a year, roughly $3,662 at the November 8 exchange rate.

US-listed crypto stocks showed little reaction. Coinbase ( NASDAQ:COIN | COIN Price Prediction ) fell 1.5% to $134.76 on November 6, while Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) dipped 0.3% to $128.93. Bitcoin trades at $75,662 and Ethereum at $2,226 today. So can a cap this small move either coin’s price?

The regulation has been officially released, naming the three cryptocurrencies eligible for purchase, the start date, and the cap for each intermediary. All buyers will also need to pass a knowledge test before investing. Qualified investors, on the other hand, face no purchase limits.

While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain. In October, the Bank of Russia authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to provide crypto exchange services. On November 2, Moscow Exchange announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades. However, Russia hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast.

Since the 300,000-ruble cap applies to each intermediary, a buyer with accounts at several brokers could buy more than the cap in a year. That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper. Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand.

Because of OFAC sanctions, Coinbase can’t serve Russian customers, so it won’t earn any direct revenue from the new regulation. Russian buying could only help Coinbase through higher crypto prices, which could in turn lift its trading and subscription income. Against Coinbase’s third-quarter revenue of $1.22 billion, any such increase would be minimal. Our Coinbase stock outlook looks at what moves the shares.

Strategy holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers. Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access. Russia’s new rules support that view, but Strategy’s stock closely follows Bitcoin’s price. Given that the cap applies inside a sanctioned country, the rule is unlikely to meaningfully move Bitcoin’s market value.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows in the week to November 6. To offset that one week of outflows, about 350,000 Russian buyers would each need to buy the full annual cap.

History points the same way. When El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply. Similarly, the launch of Hong Kong’s spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs in April 2024 didn’t lead to sustained price gains.

Russia also plans to ban peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. So some of the new regulated buying could come from existing Russian traders moving off informal channels ahead of that ban, rather than from new investors.

On the current evidence, the 300,000-ruble cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit. Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential Russian buying.

Ethereum also trades below its 30-day low close of $2,236, and capped Russian buyers might prefer Bitcoin, the better-known coin. If Bitcoin fails to reclaim its $79,362 20-day average before Moscow Exchange’s December 1 launch, that would suggest the new rules had little effect on its price. For Ethereum, the key level is its $2,156 200-day average, about 3% below its price. Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers.

extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. The regulation has been officially released, naming the three cryptocurrencies eligible for purchase, the start date, and the cap for each intermediary. All buyers will also need to pass a knowledge test before investing. Qualified investors, on the other hand, face no purchase limits. While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain. In October, the Bank of Russia authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to provide crypto exchange services. On November 2, Moscow Exchange announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades. However, Russia hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast. Since the 300,000-ruble cap applies to each intermediary, a buyer with accounts at several brokers could buy more than the cap in a year. That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper. Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand. Because of OFAC sanctions, Coinbase can’t serve Russian customers, so it won’t earn any direct revenue from the new regulation. Russian buying could only help Coinbase through higher crypto prices, which could in turn lift its trading and subscription income. Against Coinbase’s third-quarter revenue of $1.22 billion, any such increase would be minimal. Our Coinbase stock outlook looks at what moves the shares. Strategy holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers. Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access. Russia’s new rules support that view, but Strategy’s stock closely follows Bitcoin’s price. Given that the cap applies inside a sanctioned country, the rule is unlikely to meaningfully move Bitcoin’s market value. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows in the week to November 6. To offset that one week of outflows, about 350,000 Russian buyers would each need to buy the full annual cap. History points the same way. When El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply. Similarly, the launch of Hong Kong’s spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs in April 2024 didn’t lead to sustained price gains. Russia also plans to ban peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. So some of the new regulated buying could come from existing Russian traders moving off informal channels ahead of that ban, rather than from new investors. On the current evidence, the 300,000-ruble cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit. Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential Russian buying. If Bitcoin fails to reclaim its $79,362 20-day average before Moscow Exchange’s December 1 launch, that would suggest the new rules had little effect on its price. For Ethereum, the key level is its $2,156 200-day average, about 3% below its price. Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers. Russia’s central bank opened the crypto market to retail investors. Under a new Bank of Russia regulation, investors who aren’t classified as professional buyers can start buying Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), and the Tether ( CRYPTO:USDT ) stablecoin from November 17. However, purchases through any one intermediary are capped at 300,000 rubles a year, roughly $3,662 at the November 8 exchange rate.

US-listed crypto stocks showed little reaction. Coinbase ( NASDAQ:COIN | COIN Price Prediction ) fell 1.5% to $134.76 on November 6, while Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) dipped 0.3% to $128.93. Bitcoin trades at $75,662 and Ethereum at $2,226 today. So can a cap this small move either coin’s price?

The regulation has been officially released, naming the three cryptocurrencies eligible for purchase, the start date, and the cap for each intermediary. All buyers will also need to pass a knowledge test before investing. Qualified investors, on the other hand, face no purchase limits.

While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain. In October, the Bank of Russia authorized Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to provide crypto exchange services. On November 2, Moscow Exchange announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades. However, Russia hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast.

Since the 300,000-ruble cap applies to each intermediary, a buyer with accounts at several brokers could buy more than the cap in a year. That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper. Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand.

Because of OFAC sanctions, Coinbase can’t serve Russian customers, so it won’t earn any direct revenue from the new regulation. Russian buying could only help Coinbase through higher crypto prices, which could in turn lift its trading and subscription income. Against Coinbase’s third-quarter revenue of $1.22 billion, any such increase would be minimal. Our Coinbase stock outlook looks at what moves the shares.

Strategy holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers. Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access. Russia’s new rules support that view, but Strategy’s stock closely follows Bitcoin’s price. Given that the cap applies inside a sanctioned country, the rule is unlikely to meaningfully move Bitcoin’s market value.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $1.28 billion in net outflows in the week to November 6. To offset that one week of outflows, about 350,000 Russian buyers would each need to buy the full annual cap.

History points the same way. When El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply. Similarly, the launch of Hong Kong’s spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs in April 2024 didn’t lead to sustained price gains.

Russia also plans to ban peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. So some of the new regulated buying could come from existing Russian traders moving off informal channels ahead of that ban, rather than from new investors.

On the current evidence, the 300,000-ruble cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit. Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential Russian buying.

Ethereum also trades below its 30-day low close of $2,236, and capped Russian buyers might prefer Bitcoin, the better-known coin. If Bitcoin fails to reclaim its $79,362 20-day average before Moscow Exchange’s December 1 launch, that would suggest the new rules had little effect on its price. For Ethereum, the key level is its $2,156 200-day average, about 3% below its price. Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers.

extraction.body: It's a historic Sunday at the World Wide Technology Championship . Blades Brown, the 19-year-old from Tennessee, shot a final-round 63 to come from seven behind and win his first PGA Tour event, and he had to do so in a playoff against 23-year-old Ben James, who eagled the 72nd hole just to get into a playoff. Brown becomes the fourth-youngest winner in PGA Tour history (the youngest since World War II) and is the first teenager to win on Tour since Jordan Spieth. Brown won with a birdie on the second playoff hole. With the win, he'll also take home a seven-figure check. extraction.body: It's a historic Sunday at the World Wide Technology Championship . Blades Brown, the 19-year-old from Tennessee, shot a final-round 63 to come from seven behind and win his first PGA Tour event, and he had to do so in a playoff against 23-year-old Ben James, who eagled the 72nd hole just to get into a playoff. Brown becomes the fourth-youngest winner in PGA Tour history (the youngest since World War II) and is the first teenager to win on Tour since Jordan Spieth. Brown won with a birdie on the second playoff hole. With the win, he'll also take home a seven-figure check. Here's the breakdown of how much money each PGA Tour player earned at the World Wide Technology Championship, where there was a $6 million purse. extraction.body: Blades Brown’s Round 4 winning highlights from World Wide Technology “Wow, I feel good. I knew that I would now,” Blades Brown , probably. Regardless of who was going to emerge from the James-Brown playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship – that is, encore performances courtesy of Ben James and Blades Brown – he wouldn’t argue with that description of the emotion following what was his breakthrough victory on the PGA Tour. Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October.
It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025.
Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1.
In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29.

Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.
Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time.
Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin.
Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks.
The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations.
To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6.
Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%.
Bitcoin ETFs just suffered their worst single day since late June, and Ethereum ETFs have now bled red for 11 straight sessions.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October.
It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025.
Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1.
In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29.

Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.

Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin.

To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%.
Bitcoin ETFs just suffered their worst single day since late June, and Ethereum ETFs have now bled red for 11 straight sessions.

Bitcoin price on Sunday morning: $75,800 after a night without direction According to CoinGecko, Bitcoin stood at $75,833 early on Sunday morning, the equivalent of €68,031. That is practically unchanged from the previous day, down 2.4 percent over seven days and down 7.6 percent over 30 days. Between midnight and just before 6 am CET, the price on the US exchange Coinbase moved between $75,545 and $75,868. The range of $323 amounts to just over 0.4 percent. On Saturday, the price had traded between $75,453 and $76,152 across the whole day. Compared with our Bitcoin price report from Saturday morning, the price has barely moved: $75,812 was on the board then, about $20 more today. Friday's low of $74,722, which we named yesterday as the most important level to the downside, held. Because today is Sunday, tonight brings not only the close of a day but of an entire week. Bitcoin weekly candle: four losing weeks since the close at $86,507 A weekly candle sums up the price action from Monday to Sunday: open, high, low and close. Many traders pay more attention to this weekly close than to individual days, because it filters out the noise of a weekend or a hectic news cycle. The week runs on UTC, so it ends at 1 am CET in the night to Monday. On October 4, Bitcoin closed the week at $86,507, still up 2.4 percent at that point. Four red weeks followed: a close at $83,678 on October 11 (down 3.3 percent), at $82,007 on October 18 (down 2.0 percent), at $80,053 on October 25 (down 2.4 percent) and at $78,231 on November 1 (down 2.3 percent). On the Wednesday after the US midterms, Bitcoin climbed as high as $81,131; on Friday it fell as low as $74,722. If the price is still where it is now at midnight tonight, the fifth week closes with a loss of just over 3 percent. From the close on October 4 to today, the streak adds up to a loss of 12.4 percent. Why the weekly close counts for more than a daily close A daily close on Sunday falls in the middle of the period when the big futures exchanges are shut and order books stay thin. The weekly close, by contrast, is the line along which many funds and traders align their charts. For the price itself a single close changes little; for the market narrative it changes a great deal. Five red weeks in a row: only twice since 2017, in 2022 and in February 2026 A look back shows how rare such a streak is. The basis is Bitcoin's daily prices in dollars on the US exchange Coinbase from April 2017 to today, grouped into 498 weeks running Monday to Sunday. cryptoticker.io compiled this analysis itself on November 8, 2026. Four red weeks in a row occurred eight times in that period, most recently in May 2026. From March 28, 2022, Bitcoin lost nine weeks in a row, falling from $46,850 to $29,447, a drop of 37.1 percent. From January 19, 2026, six red weeks followed, from $93,630 to $65,769, a drop of 29.8 percent. In both earlier cases a lot of value had already gone in the first five weeks: around 18 percent in 2022 and almost 28 percent in early 2026, with individual weeks of minus 9 to minus 11 percent. The current streak stands at just over 12 percent after five weeks, and no single week has cost more than 3.3 percent. After the fifth losing week: down 41 and up 15 percent over twelve weeks What came next diverged sharply in the two cases. In 2022 the fifth red week was only the middle of the decline: four weeks later Bitcoin was 23.5 percent lower, twelve weeks later 41.3 percent lower. That period included the collapse of Terra and Luna in May and the bankruptcy of the lender Celsius in June. In February 2026, by contrast, a sixth red week followed the fifth, and then the trend turned. Four weeks after the fifth losing close, Bitcoin was 0.3 percent higher; twelve weeks later it was 14.5 percent higher. In April 2026 the price rose above $78,000 again for the first time.
