extraction.headline: Five Losing Weeks in a Row Loom as Bitcoin Price Sits at $75,800
extraction.description: Analysis: Bitcoin trades at $75,800 and looks set to close its fifth straight losing week tonight. Since 2017 that has happened only twice, and the market went lower once and higher once afterwards.

relevantPassages.text: Bitcoin is trading at around $75,800 on Sunday morning, and by midnight it will be clear whether this becomes the fifth losing week in a row.
Bitcoin weekly candle: four losing weeks since the close at $86,507 A weekly candle sums up the price action from Monday to Sunday: open, high, low and close.
In both earlier cases a lot of value had already gone in the first five weeks: around 18 percent in 2022 and almost 28 percent in early 2026, with individual weeks of minus 9 to minus 11 percent.
The current streak stands at just over 12 percent after five weeks, and no single week has cost more than 3.3 percent.
In 2022 the fifth red week was only the middle of the decline: four weeks later Bitcoin was 23.5 percent lower, twelve weeks later 41.3 percent lower.

If you hold Bitcoin or are planning to buy, you will find the overnight numbers here, the weekly record since early October, the comparison with 2022 and February 2026, last week's fund flows and the dates that matter from Monday.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October.
It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025.
Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1.
In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29.

Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.
Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time.
Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin.
Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks.
The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations.
To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6.
Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%.
Bitcoin ETFs just suffered their worst single day since late June, and Ethereum ETFs have now bled red for 11 straight sessions.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October. It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025. Over the past four weeks, each week closed lower than the one before. Bitcoin started at $86,507 on October 4 and dropped to $78,231 by November 1, culminating in a 2.28% loss that last week. Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1. So, what followed that Bitcoin losing streak, and does the current situation resemble it? Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which are funds that hold Bitcoin and trade on stock exchanges like regular stocks, saw significant outflows totaling $1.28 billion in the week ending November 6. When investors pull out more ETF shares than they purchase, the funds must sell Bitcoin, turning a consistent buyer into a seller. According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6. The only day with net inflows was November 4, when the funds took in $74.6 million. On November 6, Bitcoin closed at $75,775, marking its lowest closing price in the past month amid heavy ETF selling for two consecutive days. This trend of selling started earlier, with the funds reporting a $643.3 million outflow on October 30, the largest one-day exit since at least October 9. The flow of money and the price movement often affect each other. When prices fall, ETF holders may feel compelled to sell, further driving prices down. Additionally, Bitcoin’s weekly trading volume has increased over the past three weeks leading up to November 8, indicating that sellers are becoming more active as the price continues to drop. Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin. Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks. The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations. In early 2026, Bitcoin faced six weeks of losses, dropping from $93,634 on January 18 to $65,769 on March 1, with a low of $60,001 reached in the week ending February 8. Four weeks later, on March 29, it closed at $65,957, nearly unchanged. By eight weeks after the streak ended, it rose to $78,674 on April 26, a gain of about 20% from the end of the losing streak. In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29. Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded. Neither of these situations marked a lasting recovery. The rebound from the spring 2026 drop eventually faded, leading to Bitcoin’s lowest close in a year at $58,566 on June 30. Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time. Now, Bitcoin has a new set of buyers due to these ETFs, but they have also contributed to the current sell-off. Bitcoin is currently trading below its 20-day moving average of $79,362 and its 50-day average of $81,889. This means most buyers from the past two months are facing losses. It remains about 3% above its 200-day average of $73,194, a benchmark many traders use to tell a pullback apart from a bear market. Each bounce this week, including a high of $81,131, has struggled to exceed the 50-day average. Moreover, large traders have shifted their stance regarding Bitcoin. On-chain analytics firm Glassnode noted that major traders on Hyperliquid began to take net short positions on October 27, after holding long positions for seven months, and have continued to add to those shorts. A short position profits when prices fall, indicating that they expect further declines. Bitcoin’s dominance , its share of the overall cryptocurrency market, remains at 60%. Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%. Over the past month, though, Bitcoin’s 8.31% loss is still smaller than Ethereum’s 10.19% and Solana’s 18.16%. Bitcoin’s deeper trading market and a larger base of ETF investors imply that when market players reduce their exposure to cryptocurrency, they typically sell the smaller and more volatile coins first. Ethereum’s relative strength this past week may appear to be a pause in that trend, but it too remains down more than Bitcoin over the month. A quick recovery from this downturn appears unlikely. In previous long losing streaks, it took at least a month to find a floor, and so far, there has been no sign of returning buyers in the market. Over the past four weeks, each week closed lower than the one before. Bitcoin started at $86,507 on October 4 and dropped to $78,231 by November 1, culminating in a 2.28% loss that last week. Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1. So, what followed that Bitcoin losing streak, and does the current situation resemble it?

Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which are funds that hold Bitcoin and trade on stock exchanges like regular stocks, saw significant outflows totaling $1.28 billion in the week ending November 6. When investors pull out more ETF shares than they purchase, the funds must sell Bitcoin, turning a consistent buyer into a seller.

According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6. The only day with net inflows was November 4, when the funds took in $74.6 million.

On November 6, Bitcoin closed at $75,775, marking its lowest closing price in the past month amid heavy ETF selling for two consecutive days. This trend of selling started earlier, with the funds reporting a $643.3 million outflow on October 30, the largest one-day exit since at least October 9.

The flow of money and the price movement often affect each other. When prices fall, ETF holders may feel compelled to sell, further driving prices down. Additionally, Bitcoin’s weekly trading volume has increased over the past three weeks leading up to November 8, indicating that sellers are becoming more active as the price continues to drop.

Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin. Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks. The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations.

In early 2026, Bitcoin faced six weeks of losses, dropping from $93,634 on January 18 to $65,769 on March 1, with a low of $60,001 reached in the week ending February 8. Four weeks later, on March 29, it closed at $65,957, nearly unchanged. By eight weeks after the streak ended, it rose to $78,674 on April 26, a gain of about 20% from the end of the losing streak.

In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29. Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.

Neither of these situations marked a lasting recovery. The rebound from the spring 2026 drop eventually faded, leading to Bitcoin’s lowest close in a year at $58,566 on June 30. Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time. Now, Bitcoin has a new set of buyers due to these ETFs, but they have also contributed to the current sell-off.

Bitcoin is currently trading below its 20-day moving average of $79,362 and its 50-day average of $81,889. This means most buyers from the past two months are facing losses. It remains about 3% above its 200-day average of $73,194, a benchmark many traders use to tell a pullback apart from a bear market. Each bounce this week, including a high of $81,131, has struggled to exceed the 50-day average.

Moreover, large traders have shifted their stance regarding Bitcoin. On-chain analytics firm Glassnode noted that major traders on Hyperliquid began to take net short positions on October 27, after holding long positions for seven months, and have continued to add to those shorts. A short position profits when prices fall, indicating that they expect further declines.

Bitcoin’s dominance , its share of the overall cryptocurrency market, remains at 60%. Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%. Over the past month, though, Bitcoin’s 8.31% loss is still smaller than Ethereum’s 10.19% and Solana’s 18.16%.

Bitcoin’s deeper trading market and a larger base of ETF investors imply that when market players reduce their exposure to cryptocurrency, they typically sell the smaller and more volatile coins first. Ethereum’s relative strength this past week may appear to be a pause in that trend, but it too remains down more than Bitcoin over the month.

A quick recovery from this downturn appears unlikely. In previous long losing streaks, it took at least a month to find a floor, and so far, there has been no sign of returning buyers in the market. To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

extraction.body: LOS CABOS, Mexico (AP) — Blades Brown became the youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years Sunday when the 19-year-old rallied from a seven-shot deficit with a 9-under 63 and beat Ben James with a birdie on the second playoff hole in the World Wide Technology Championship. Brown became the youngest winner since Charles Kocsis won the Michigan Open in 1931 when he was 18, a tournament that was considered a regional event in the early years of the PGA. James lost a four-shot lead going into the final round at El Cardonal at Diamante and then showed his moxie by smoking a 285-yard shot into 20 feet on the par-5 18th and making eagle to salvage a 70 and force the playoff. But he missed an 8-foot putt on the second playoff hole, and Brown made his 3-footer. ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates (AP) — Jon Rahm fought off Ryder Cup teammates Rory McIlroy and Tyrrell Hatton to win the Abu Dhabi Championship on Sunday for his first European tour title in four years and his first start since the demise of LIV Golf. Rahm shot 5-under 67 at Yas Links and finished two shots ahead of Hatton (68) and four ahead of McIlroy (69) in the first of the two season-ending playoff tournaments in the United Arab Emirates. This was Rahm's first event in seven weeks, during which time his wife gave birth to their fourth child and he finalized his departure from LIV Golf. The victory moves him back into the top 10 in the world ranking. McIlroy moved to No. 2 in the Race to Dubai, 534 points behind Eugenio Chacarra. The title will be decided next week at the DP World Tour Championship, which McIlroy has won three times. OMITAMA, Japan (AP) — Shuri Sakuma became the fifth Japanese player to win on the LPGA Tour this season, closing with an 8-under 64 for a four-shot victory in the Toto Classic. Sakuma won for the fifth time on the Japan LPGA this year, after a four-win season in 2025. The victory makes her eligible to join the LPGA Tour. She finished at 20-under 268. Aki Iwai, who had a one-shot lead going into the final round, closed with a 71 to finish second. Erika Hara finished a career-best third after a 70 at the Taiheiyo Club north of Tokyo, moving Hara to No. 32 in the Race to CME Globe. Yuta Ikeda closed with a 4-under 67l and won a three-man playoff to capture the ACN Championship on the Japan Tour. Ikeda won after Kohei Okada made bogey on the first playoff hole, and Ryunosoke Furukawa Kohei failed to match Ikeda's par on the fourth playoff hole. ... Ana Pelaez Trivino rallied from five shots behind with a 9-under 64, winning the Aramco China Championship by three shots over Mimi Rhodes on the Ladies European Tour. ... Louis Albertse closed with a 4-under 68 for a three-shot victory in the Telkom PGA Championship on the Sunshine Tour in South Africa. ... Jean Hugo closed with a 7-under 65 to win the European Senior Masters in Spain for his third win in as many starts on the Legends Tour. ... Hyunjo Yoo shot 4-under 68 and won the Daebo HausD Championship by one shot on the Korea LPGA.

extraction.body: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo. In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times. In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour. James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours. While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh. Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.” Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories. Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years. Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.” It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race. Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler. When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler. Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too. James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes. “Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.” Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under. Brown had birdied nine of his first 15 holes, three coming from about 12 feet and two more from around 25 feet – not surprising considering Brown is used to converting from deep; his mother, Rhonda, made the first 3-pointer in WNBA history while her son was a standout guard in high school. Blades claims he once almost made 50 consecutive 3’s during a shootaround. Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt. “I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.” James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole. “If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’” CABO SAN LUCAS, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 08: Blades Brown of the United States celebrates with his dad, Parke Brown, after winning the final round of the World Wide Technology Championship 2026 at El Cardonal at Diamante on November 08, 2026 in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) On the first playoff hole, No. 18, James hit his second shot nearly to the same spot, just a few feet farther away. Brown was almost in the exact spot that James was in regulation, at about 20 feet from the cup. James’ eagle bid tried to curl back right into the hole but failed, Brown’s try came up a few revolutions short, and the two headed back to the 18th tee. Both players nearly hit their next tee shots into their own divots, though neither found the green in two this time, both missing short and right. James nearly chipped in, but he ran it too far past for his balky putter and whiffed on the 6-footer. Brown cozied one close and didn’t miss his opportunity to break through. “I’ve known Ben since we were amateur golfers and he’s just such a great player,” Brown said. “I’m sure we’re going to be battling it out for years to come.” Not long after he shook James’ hand on the final green, Brown was getting bear-hugged by his dad, Parke, who rarely skips a tournament. Parke actually missed two while undergoing chemotherapy a few years ago for hairy cell leukemia. Parke was initially misdiagnosed and given months to live, but he now manages the treatable disease while traveling the world with his only son, who is now a PGA Tour champion with the golf world seemingly at his fingertips. Blades, who inherited his dad’s infectious energy and charisma, balks somewhat at the projections, which are even loftier now. “I’ve got a long way to go,” Brown said. “There’s so many shots that I want to learn. Golf, I don’t think you ever can master, but I’m going to do my best to see how close we can get.” © Copyright 2026 Golf Channel. All rights reserved.

Jean Hugo closed with a 7-under 65 to win the European Senior Masters in Spain for his third win in as many starts on the Legends Tour. ... extraction.body: It was a matchup of budding superstars in Sunday’s playoff at the World Wide Technology Championship in Cabo. In one corner stood Ben James, the 23-year-old rookie out of Virginia who is the most recent PGA Tour University No. 1 and one of only five players in NCAA history to be named a first-team All-American four times. In the other: Blades Brown, the teen wonder who eschewed college to jump straight to the pros and just a few weeks ago locked up his PGA Tour card for 2027 via the Korn Ferry Tour. James began the final round leading the field by four strokes before his weekend struggles on the greens persisted and allowed the freewheeling Brown, seven behind to start the day, to rocket into the clubhouse lead with a 9-under 63, his sixth sub-64 round of the year between both tours. While James delivered some heroics on his 72nd hole, this par-5 18th at Diamante’s El Cardonal course – he flushed 3-wood 289 yards to 20 feet and hooped the eagle putt to force overtime – Brown had the last laugh. Brown birdied the second extra hole after a short miss by James to capture his maiden PGA Tour title and become the fourth youngest winner in PGA Tour history – and youngest in the post-World War II era – at 19 years, 5 months, 18 days old. “It hasn’t set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner,” Brown said. “Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right? I mean, it still hasn’t sunk in yet. I just go back to, you know, 5-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I’m now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind blowing.” Brown is nearly six months younger than Jordan Spieth was when Spieth won the 2013 John Deere Classic, and only Charles Kocsis (1931), Harry Cooper (1923) and Ralph Guldahl (1931) were younger than Brown for their victories. Brown’s breakthrough comes on a layout designed by Woods, whom Brown joined in exclusive company as the only players, along with Bobby Clampett, to garner medalist honors at both the U.S. Amateur and U.S. Junior Amateur. When a 16-year-old Brown medaled at the 2023 U.S. Amateur, he broke Bobby Jones’ mark of youngest U.S. Amateur medalist by two years. Age, though, has never been of concern to Brown, who has always maintained, “The golf ball doesn’t care how old you are.” It was nearly two years ago that Brown announced he’d forego college and turn professional at just 17 years old. He secured full Korn Ferry Tour privileges by the end of last year before becoming that tour’s youngest graduate with a ninth-place finish in this season’s points race. Brown, of course, has also gained significant experience on the big tour. After playing eight events in 2025, Brown locked up special temporary status this season, and entering this week’s event in Cabo, his 13th of the year, he boasted eight top-25s, including a solo third in Puerto Rico and a T-18 at the American Express, where he shot 60 in the second round and earned a spot in the final group alongside world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler. When Scheffler was announced on the first tee that Sunday back in January in Palm Springs, Brown admitted that he accidentally started clapping before his caddie had to remind him that he was competing against Scheffler. Scheffler will see a lot more of Brown in the future – and James, too. James now has five top-5 finishes since turning pro this summer. He seemed to be on cruise control until his putter fell apart on the weekend – he was gaining 0.292 strokes per round on the greens coming into this tournament, a byproduct of his switch to the reverse claw grip two summers ago, but he lost more than four strokes over his final 36 holes in Cabo, a number that was closer to 4.5 before the eagle make. James bogeyed three of his first eight holes and carded another bogey at No. 13 that dropped him two back and delivered what seemed like a huge blow to his victory hopes. “Definitely a lot of emotions,” James said afterward. “I mean, it was a long day. I fought really, really hard. Really poor start, poor front nine. Drove the green on 10, three-putted. I couldn’t really get anything going.” Denny McCarthy, one of the best putters of the past decade, had some issues with the flatstick as well. Before McCarthy whiffed on a 6-footer and double-bogeyed the par-4 17th, McCarthy’s three-putt from 42 feet at the par-4 15th knocked him out of the share of the lead with Brown, who teed off on the par-5 18th all alone at 22 under. Brown had birdied nine of his first 15 holes, three coming from about 12 feet and two more from around 25 feet – not surprising considering Brown is used to converting from deep; his mother, Rhonda, made the first 3-pointer in WNBA history while her son was a standout guard in high school. Blades claims he once almost made 50 consecutive 3’s during a shootaround. Brown’s 10th birdie of the day came on his 72nd hole, the par-5 18th, where Brown hit his second shot 241 yards to just shy of the green. He then pitched to 6 feet and calmly, like he’s been on the PGA Tour for decades, sank the putt. “I feel like he might be the best out of all the younger guys that I played with,” said Michael Kim, who finished solo third, a shot out of the playoff. “The way his club makes contact with the ball, that’s kind of only those that are true, true talents of the game can kind of make that contact.” James followed Brown’s celebratory fist pump with one of his own. In fact, as Brown was hitting balls on the range, James poured in his eagle and held his clenched right fist all the way to retrieve his ball from the hole. “If you would have said any player had to make eagle on the last hole, I’d be like, man, we’re obviously in the clear,” Brown said. “But Ben James, I knew that he had it in him. I actually didn’t see the putt go in, but I heard a big roar. When I heard that, I was like, ‘All right, it’s go time.’” CABO SAN LUCAS, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 08: Blades Brown of the United States celebrates with his dad, Parke Brown, after winning the final round of the World Wide Technology Championship 2026 at El Cardonal at Diamante on November 08, 2026 in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. (Photo by Orlando Ramirez/Getty Images) On the first playoff hole, No. 18, James hit his second shot nearly to the same spot, just a few feet farther away. Brown was almost in the exact spot that James was in regulation, at about 20 feet from the cup. James’ eagle bid tried to curl back right into the hole but failed, Brown’s try came up a few revolutions short, and the two headed back to the 18th tee. Both players nearly hit their next tee shots into their own divots, though neither found the green in two this time, both missing short and right. James nearly chipped in, but he ran it too far past for his balky putter and whiffed on the 6-footer. Brown cozied one close and didn’t miss his opportunity to break through. “I’ve known Ben since we were amateur golfers and he’s just such a great player,” Brown said. “I’m sure we’re going to be battling it out for years to come.” Not long after he shook James’ hand on the final green, Brown was getting bear-hugged by his dad, Parke, who rarely skips a tournament. Parke actually missed two while undergoing chemotherapy a few years ago for hairy cell leukemia. Parke was initially misdiagnosed and given months to live, but he now manages the treatable disease while traveling the world with his only son, who is now a PGA Tour champion with the golf world seemingly at his fingertips. Blades, who inherited his dad’s infectious energy and charisma, balks somewhat at the projections, which are even loftier now. “I’ve got a long way to go,” Brown said. “There’s so many shots that I want to learn. Golf, I don’t think you ever can master, but I’m going to do my best to see how close we can get.” © Copyright 2026 Golf Channel. All rights reserved.

sources.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware
passages: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military. This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication. Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces. The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military. Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are. Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center. President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones. An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.

This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication.

Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.

The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military.

Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are.

Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones.

story.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware

facts.text: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

sources.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware
passages: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication.
